# FP Jargon - Full Reference

> Complete catalog of 75 functional programming concepts, morphisms, algebraic structures, and category theory terms with JavaScript ES2015 examples.
> Source: https://github.com/hemanth/functional-programming-jargon
> Live app: https://hemanth.github.io/functional-programming-jargon/

## Arity

- Category: Core Functions
- ID: #arity
- Aliases: unary, binary, ternary, nullary, variadic
- Related concepts: #currying

### Definition
The number of arguments a function takes. From words like unary, binary, ternary, etc.

### Code Examples

```js
const sum = (a, b) => a + b
// The arity of sum is 2 (binary)
const inc = a => a + 1
// The arity of inc is 1 (unary)
const zero = () => 0
// The arity of zero is 0 (nullary)
```

---

## Higher-Order Functions (HOF)

- Category: Core Functions
- ID: #higher-order-functions-hof
- Aliases: hof, higher order function
- Related concepts: #partial-application, #point-free-style, #functional-combinator, #closure, #predicate, #function-composition, #continuation, #trampoline

### Definition
A function which takes a function as an argument and/or returns a function.

### Code Examples

```js
const filter = (predicate, xs) => xs.filter(predicate)
```

```js
const is = (type) => (x) => Object(x) instanceof type
```

```js
filter(is(Number), [0, '1', 2, null]) // [0, 2]
```

---

## Closure

- Category: Core Functions
- ID: #closure
- Related concepts: #lambda, #higher-order-functions-hof

### Definition
A closure is a scope which captures local variables of a function for access even after the execution has moved out of the block in which it is defined. This allows the values in the closure to be accessed by returned functions.

### Code Examples

```js
const addTo = x => y => x + y
const addToFive = addTo(5)
addToFive(3) // => 8
```

---

## Partial Application

- Category: Composition & Flow
- ID: #partial-application
- Related concepts: #currying, #higher-order-functions-hof

### Definition
Partially applying a function means creating a new function by pre-filling some of the arguments to the original function.

### Code Examples

```js
// Helper to create partially applied functions
// Takes a function and some arguments
const partial = (f, ...args) =>
  // returns a function that takes the rest of the arguments
  (...moreArgs) =>
    // and calls the original function with all of them
    f(...args, ...moreArgs)

// Something to apply
const add3 = (a, b, c) => a + b + c

// Partially applying `2` and `3` to `add3` gives you a one-argument function
const fivePlus = partial(add3, 2, 3) // (c) => 2 + 3 + c

fivePlus(4) // 9
```

```js
const add1More = add3.bind(null, 2, 3) // (c) => 2 + 3 + c
```

---

## Currying

- Category: Composition & Flow
- ID: #currying
- Aliases: curried
- Related concepts: #partial-application, #arity, #auto-currying, #point-free-style, #constant-function

### Definition
The process of converting a function that takes multiple arguments into a function that takes them one at a time.

### Code Examples

```js
const sum = (a, b) => a + b

const curriedSum = (a) => (b) => a + b

curriedSum(40)(2) // 42.

const add2 = curriedSum(2) // (b) => 2 + b

add2(10) // 12
```

---

## Auto Currying

- Category: Composition & Flow
- ID: #auto-currying
- Related concepts: #currying

### Definition
Transforming a function that takes multiple arguments into one that if given less than its correct number of arguments returns a function that takes the rest. When the function gets the correct number of arguments it is then evaluated.

### Code Examples

```js
const add = (x, y) => x + y

const curriedAdd = _.curry(add)
curriedAdd(1, 2) // 3
curriedAdd(1) // (y) => 1 + y
curriedAdd(1)(2) // 3
```

---

## Function Composition

- Category: Composition & Flow
- ID: #function-composition
- Related concepts: #point-free-style, #category, #higher-order-functions-hof, #lens, #semigroupoid

### Definition
The act of putting two functions together to form a third function where the output of one function is the input of the other. This is one of the most important ideas of functional programming.

### Code Examples

```js
const compose = (f, g) => (a) => f(g(a)) // Definition
const floorAndToString = compose((val) => val.toString(), Math.floor) // Usage
floorAndToString(121.212121) // '121'
```

---

## Continuation

- Category: Composition & Flow
- ID: #continuation
- Related concepts: #higher-order-functions-hof, #trampoline, #algebraic-effects

### Definition
At any given point in a program, the part of the code that's yet to be executed is known as a continuation.

### Code Examples

```js
const printAsString = (num) => console.log(`Given ${num}`)

const addOneAndContinue = (num, cc) => {
  const result = num + 1
  cc(result)
}

addOneAndContinue(2, printAsString) // 'Given 3'
```

```js
const continueProgramWith = (data) => {
  // Continues program with data
}

readFileAsync('path/to/file', (err, response) => {
  if (err) {
    // handle error
    return
  }
  continueProgramWith(response)
})
```

---

## IO

- Category: Composition & Flow
- ID: #io
- Aliases: task, effect container, side effect recipe
- Related concepts: #side-effects, #monad, #lazy-evaluation, #thunk, #free-monad, #value

### Definition
A pure data structure that encapsulates a side effect. Instead of performing the effect immediately, IO wraps the action in a nullary function (thunk), allowing effectful operations to be transformed, chained, and composed as pure values without actually executing them until explicitly triggered.

### Code Examples

```js
const IO = (run) => ({
  run,
  map: (f) => IO(() => f(run())),
  chain: (f) => IO(() => f(run()).run())
})

// Pure description - nothing executes yet
const readTimestamp = IO(() => Date.now())
const formatted = readTimestamp.map((ts) => new Date(ts).toISOString())

// Side effect executes only when calling .run()
formatted.run()
```

---

## Trampoline

- Category: Core Functions
- ID: #trampoline
- Aliases: thunk loop, tail recursion optimization
- Related concepts: #higher-order-functions-hof, #continuation, #thunk

### Definition
A mechanism that enables deep or mutually recursive functions to run without exceeding the maximum call stack limit.

### Code Examples

```js
const trampoline = (fn) => (...args) => {
  let result = fn(...args)
  while (typeof result === 'function') {
    result = result()
  }
  return result
}

// Without trampoline: sumBelow(1000000) throws "Maximum call stack size exceeded"
const sumBelow = (n, acc = 0) =>
  n === 0
    ? acc
    : () => sumBelow(n - 1, acc + n) // returns a thunk instead of recursing directly

const safeSum = trampoline(sumBelow)
safeSum(1000000) // 500000500000
```

---

## Thunk

- Category: Core Functions
- ID: #thunk
- Aliases: deferred computation, nullary function, lazy thunk
- Related concepts: #lazy-evaluation, #trampoline, #io

### Definition
A nullary function (a function taking zero arguments) that wraps an expression to delay its evaluation until called. Thunks are the fundamental mechanism for implementing lazy evaluation, trampolines, and deferred side effects.

### Code Examples

```js
// An eager calculation executes immediately:
// const data = expensiveCalculation()

// A thunk wraps the expression in a function, deferring execution:
const thunk = () => 42 * 2

// The expression is only evaluated when explicitly called:
thunk() // 84
```

---

## Algebraic Effects

- Category: Composition & Flow
- ID: #algebraic-effects
- Related concepts: #continuation, #side-effects, #free-monad

### Definition
A computational effect system that separates the invocation of an effect from its handling. Rather than coupling a function directly to its runtime environment, the function "performs" an effect operation (such as reading state, requesting configuration, or logging). An enclosing "handler" intercepts the performed effect and supplies the result, with the ability to resume or abort the computation—generalizing exceptions, async/await, and generators without requiring complex monad transformer stacks.

### Code Examples

```js
// Generators model delimited continuations / algebraic effects:
const perform = (effect) => ({ [Symbol.for('effect')]: true, effect })

// Program performs effects without knowing who handles them:
function * fetchUserProfile (userId) {
  const config = yield perform({ type: 'ask_config' })
  yield perform({ type: 'log', message: `Fetching user ${userId} from ${config.apiUrl}` })
  return { id: userId, name: 'Alice' }
}

// Effect handler interprets effects and resumes the computation:
const handle = (generator, handlers) => {
  const iter = generator()
  const step = (value) => {
    const { done, value: yielded } = iter.next(value)
    if (done) return yielded
    if (yielded && yielded[Symbol.for('effect')]) {
      const { type } = yielded.effect
      if (handlers[type]) {
        return handlers[type](yielded.effect, (resumeVal) => step(resumeVal))
      }
    }
    return step(yielded)
  }
  return step()
}

// Running with an interpreter / handler:
handle(
  () => fetchUserProfile(42),
  {
    ask_config: (effect, resume) => resume({ apiUrl: 'https://api.test.local' }),
    log: (effect, resume) => {
      console.log(effect.message)
      return resume()
    }
  }
)
```

---

## Pure Function

- Category: Core Functions
- ID: #pure-function
- Aliases: deterministic function, purity
- Related concepts: #side-effects, #referential-transparency, #idempotence, #equational-reasoning, #function, #lazy-evaluation, #lens, #memoization, #either

### Definition
A function is pure if the return value is only determined by its input values, and does not produce side effects. The function must always return the same result when given the same input.

### Code Examples

```js
const greet = (name) => `Hi, ${name}`

greet('Brianne') // 'Hi, Brianne'
```

```js
window.name = 'Brianne'

const greet = () => `Hi, ${window.name}`

greet() // "Hi, Brianne"
```

```js
let greeting

const greet = (name) => {
  greeting = `Hi, ${name}`
}

greet('Brianne')
greeting // "Hi, Brianne"
```

---

## Side effects

- Category: Purity & Reasoning
- ID: #side-effects
- Related concepts: #pure-function, #io, #algebraic-effects, #memoization, #function

### Definition
A function or expression is said to have a side effect if apart from returning a value, it interacts with (reads from or writes to) external mutable state.

### Code Examples

```js
const differentEveryTime = new Date()
```

```js
console.log('IO is a side effect!')
```

---

## Idempotence

- Category: Purity & Reasoning
- ID: #idempotence
- Related concepts: #pure-function, #memoization

### Definition
A function is idempotent if reapplying it to its result does not produce a different result.

### Code Examples

```js
Math.abs(Math.abs(10))
```

```js
sort(sort(sort([2, 1])))
```

---

## Point-Free Style

- Category: Composition & Flow
- ID: #point-free-style
- Aliases: tacit programming, tacit, point-free, pointfree
- Related concepts: #currying, #function-composition, #higher-order-functions-hof, #functional-combinator

### Definition
Writing functions where the definition does not explicitly identify the arguments used. This style usually requires currying or other Higher-Order functions. A.K.A Tacit programming.

### Code Examples

```js
// Given
const map = (fn) => (list) => list.map(fn)
const add = (a) => (b) => a + b

// Then

// Not point-free - `numbers` is an explicit argument
const incrementAll = (numbers) => map(add(1))(numbers)

// Point-free - The list is an implicit argument
const incrementAll2 = map(add(1))
```

---

## Predicate

- Category: Core Functions
- ID: #predicate
- Related concepts: #higher-order-functions-hof, #contravariant-functor

### Definition
A predicate is a function that returns true or false for a given value. A common use of a predicate is as the callback for array filter.

### Code Examples

```js
const predicate = (a) => a > 2

;[1, 2, 3, 4].filter(predicate) // [3, 4]
```

---

## Contracts

- Category: Purity & Reasoning
- ID: #contracts
- Related concepts: #type-signatures

### Definition
A contract specifies the obligations and guarantees of the behavior from a function or expression at runtime. This acts as a set of rules that are expected from the input and output of a function or expression, and errors are generally reported whenever a contract is violated.

### Code Examples

```js
// Define our contract : int -> boolean
const contract = (input) => {
  if (typeof input === 'number') return true
  throw new Error('Contract violated: expected int -> boolean')
}

const addOne = (num) => contract(num) && num + 1

addOne(2) // 3
addOne('some string') // Contract violated: expected int -> boolean
```

---

## Category

- Category: Category & Morphisms
- ID: #category
- Related concepts: #morphism, #function-composition, #natural-transformation, #semigroupoid

### Definition
A category in category theory is a collection of objects and morphisms between them. In programming, typically types act as the objects and functions as morphisms.

### Code Examples

```js
class Max {
  constructor (a) {
    this.a = a
  }

  id () {
    return this
  }

  compose (b) {
    return this.a > b.a ? this : b
  }

  toString () {
    return `Max(${this.a})`
  }
}

new Max(2).compose(new Max(3)).compose(new Max(5)).id().id() // => Max(5)
```

---

## Semigroupoid

- Category: Category & Morphisms
- ID: #semigroupoid
- Related concepts: #category, #function-composition, #semigroup

### Definition
An algebraic structure with objects and morphisms that can be associatively composed, but does not guarantee the existence of an identity morphism for each object.

### Code Examples

```js
const Semigroupoid = (fn) => ({
  run: fn,
  compose: (other) => Semigroupoid((x) => fn(other.run(x)))
})

const toUpper = Semigroupoid((s) => s.toUpperCase())
const exclaim = Semigroupoid((s) => `${s}!`)

const loudGreeting = exclaim.compose(toUpper)
loudGreeting.run('hello') // 'HELLO!'
```

---

## Value

- Category: Purity & Reasoning
- ID: #value
- Related concepts: #constant, #io

### Definition
Anything that can be assigned to a variable.

### Code Examples

```js
5
Object.freeze({ name: 'John', age: 30 }) // The `freeze` function enforces immutability.
;(a) => a
;[1]
undefined
```

---

## Constant

- Category: Purity & Reasoning
- ID: #constant
- Related concepts: #referential-transparency, #constant-function, #value

### Definition
A variable that cannot be reassigned once defined.

### Code Examples

```js
const five = 5
const john = Object.freeze({ name: 'John', age: 30 })
```

```js
john.age + five === ({ name: 'John', age: 30 }).age + 5
```

---

## Constant Function

- Category: Purity & Reasoning
- ID: #constant-function
- Related concepts: #constant, #constant-functor, #currying

### Definition
A curried function that ignores its second argument:

### Code Examples

```js
const constant = a => () => a

;[1, 2].map(constant(0)) // => [0, 0]
```

---

## Constant Functor

- Category: Algebraic Structures
- ID: #constant-functor
- Related concepts: #constant-function, #constant-monad, #functor

### Definition
Object whose map doesn't transform the contents. See Functor.

### Code Examples

```js
Constant(1).map(n => n + 1) // => Constant(1)
```

---

## Constant Monad

- Category: Algebraic Structures
- ID: #constant-monad
- Related concepts: #constant-functor, #monad

### Definition
Object whose chain doesn't transform the contents. See Monad.

### Code Examples

```js
Constant(1).chain(n => Constant(n + 1)) // => Constant(1)
```

---

## Functor

- Category: Algebraic Structures
- ID: #functor
- Aliases: map, mappable
- Related concepts: #pointed-functor, #applicative-functor, #lift, #traversable, #bifunctor, #contravariant-functor, #natural-transformation, #free-monad, #constant-functor, #option, #monad, #monad-transformer

### Definition
An object that implements a map function that takes a function which is run on the contents of that object. A functor must adhere to two rules:

### Code Examples

```js
object.map(x => x)
```

```js
object.map(x => g(f(x)))
```

```js
object.map(f).map(g)
```

```js
Some(1).map(x => x) // = Some(1)
```

```js
const f = x => x + 1
const g = x => x * 2

Some(1).map(x => g(f(x))) // = Some(4)
Some(1).map(f).map(g) // = Some(4)
```

---

## Pointed Functor

- Category: Algebraic Structures
- ID: #pointed-functor
- Related concepts: #functor, #applicative-functor, #lift, #monad

### Definition
An object with an of function that puts any single value into it.

### Code Examples

```js
Array.of(1) // [1]
```

---

## Lift

- Category: Algebraic Structures
- ID: #lift
- Related concepts: #applicative-functor, #functor, #pointed-functor

### Definition
Lifting is when you take a value and put it into an object like a functor. If you lift a function into an Applicative Functor then you can make it work on values that are also in that functor.

### Code Examples

```js
const liftA2 = (f) => (a, b) => a.map(f).ap(b) // note it's `ap` and not `map`.

const mult = a => b => a * b

const liftedMult = liftA2(mult) // this function now works on functors like array

liftedMult([1, 2], [3]) // [3, 6]
liftA2(a => b => a + b)([1, 2], [30, 40]) // [31, 41, 32, 42]
```

```js
const increment = (x) => x + 1

lift(increment)([2]) // [3]
;[2].map(increment) // [3]
```

```js
Array.of(1) // => [1]
```

---

## Referential Transparency

- Category: Purity & Reasoning
- ID: #referential-transparency
- Aliases: referential transparent, substitution model
- Related concepts: #pure-function, #equational-reasoning, #constant, #memoization, #function

### Definition
An expression that can be replaced with its value without changing the behavior of the program is said to be referentially transparent.

### Code Examples

```js
const greet = () => 'Hello World!'
```

---

## Equational Reasoning

- Category: Purity & Reasoning
- ID: #equational-reasoning
- Aliases: algebraic reasoning
- Related concepts: #pure-function, #referential-transparency

### Definition
When an application is composed of expressions and devoid of side effects, truths about the system can be derived from the parts. You can also be confident about details of your system without having to go through every function.

### Code Examples

```js
const grainToDogs = compose(chickenIntoDogs, grainIntoChicken)
const grainToCats = compose(dogsIntoCats, grainToDogs)
```

---

## Memoization

- Category: Purity & Reasoning
- ID: #memoization
- Aliases: memoize, memoized, caching
- Related concepts: #pure-function, #referential-transparency, #idempotence, #side-effects

### Definition
An optimization technique that caches the return value of a function based on its input parameters. Memoization is only valid and safe for pure functions possessing referential transparency, because calling the function with identical arguments must always yield identical results without producing observable side effects.

### Code Examples

```js
const memoize = (fn) => {
  const cache = new Map()
  return (arg) => {
    if (!cache.has(arg)) {
      cache.set(arg, fn(arg))
    }
    return cache.get(arg)
  }
}

const factorial = memoize((n) => (n <= 1 ? 1 : n * factorial(n - 1)))
factorial(5) // Calculated: 120
factorial(5) // Retrieved from cache: 120
```

---

## Lambda

- Category: Core Functions
- ID: #lambda
- Aliases: anonymous function, arrow function
- Related concepts: #function, #closure, #lambda-calculus

### Definition
An anonymous function that can be treated like a value.

### Code Examples

```js
;(function (a) {
  return a + 1
})

;(a) => a + 1
```

```js
;[1, 2].map((a) => a + 1) // [2, 3]
```

```js
const add1 = (a) => a + 1
```

---

## Lambda Calculus

- Category: Types & Data Modeling
- ID: #lambda-calculus
- Related concepts: #lambda

### Definition
A branch of mathematics that uses functions to create a universal model of computation.

---

## Functional Combinator

- Category: Composition & Flow
- ID: #functional-combinator
- Related concepts: #point-free-style, #higher-order-functions-hof

### Definition
A higher-order function, usually curried, which returns a new function changed in some way. Functional combinators are often used in Point-Free Style to write especially terse programs.

### Code Examples

```js
// The "C" combinator takes a curried two-argument function and returns one which calls the original function with the arguments reversed.
const C = (f) => (a) => (b) => f(b)(a)

const divide = (a) => (b) => a / b

const divideBy = C(divide)

const divBy10 = divideBy(10)

divBy10(30) // => 3
```

---

## Lazy evaluation

- Category: Composition & Flow
- ID: #lazy-evaluation
- Aliases: call-by-need, deferred execution, generators
- Related concepts: #pure-function, #io, #thunk

### Definition
Lazy evaluation is a call-by-need evaluation mechanism that delays the evaluation of an expression until its value is needed. In functional languages, this allows for structures like infinite lists, which would not normally be available in an imperative language where the sequencing of commands is significant.

### Code Examples

```js
const rand = function * () {
  while (1 < 2) {
    yield Math.random()
  }
}
```

```js
const randIter = rand()
randIter.next() // Each execution gives a random value, expression is evaluated on need.
```

---

## Monoid

- Category: Algebraic Structures
- ID: #monoid
- Aliases: empty, identity, semigroup with identity
- Related concepts: #semigroup, #foldable, #alternative, #homomorphism

### Definition
An object with a function that "combines" that object with another of the same type (semigroup) which has an "identity" value.

### Code Examples

```js
1 + 1 // 2
```

```js
1 + 0 // 1
0 + 1 // 1
1 + 0 === 0 + 1
```

```js
1 + (2 + 3) === (1 + 2) + 3 // true
```

```js
;[1, 2].concat([3, 4]) // [1, 2, 3, 4]
```

```js
;[1, 2].concat([]) // [1, 2]
```

```js
0 - 4 === 4 - 0 // false
```

---

## Monad

- Category: Algebraic Structures
- ID: #monad
- Aliases: flatmap, bind, chain, return
- Related concepts: #applicative-functor, #kleisli-composition, #comonad, #option, #either, #io, #free-monad, #monad-transformer, #constant-monad, #pointed-functor, #functor

### Definition
A monad is an object with of and chain functions. chain is like map except it un-nests the resulting nested object.

### Code Examples

```js
// Implementation
Array.prototype.chain = function (f) {
  return this.reduce((acc, it) => acc.concat(f(it)), [])
}

// Usage
Array.of('cat,dog', 'fish,bird').chain((a) => a.split(',')) // ['cat', 'dog', 'fish', 'bird']

// Contrast to map
Array.of('cat,dog', 'fish,bird').map((a) => a.split(',')) // [['cat', 'dog'], ['fish', 'bird']]
```

---

## Comonad

- Category: Algebraic Structures
- ID: #comonad
- Related concepts: #monad

### Definition
An object that has extract and extend functions.

### Code Examples

```js
const CoIdentity = (v) => ({
  val: v,
  extract () {
    return this.val
  },
  extend (f) {
    return CoIdentity(f(this))
  }
})
```

```js
CoIdentity(1).extract() // 1
```

```js
CoIdentity(1).extend((co) => co.extract() + 1) // CoIdentity(2)
```

---

## Kleisli Composition

- Category: Algebraic Structures
- ID: #kleisli-composition
- Related concepts: #monad, #monad-transformer, #option

### Definition
An operation for composing two monad-returning functions (Kleisli Arrows) where they have compatible types. In Haskell this is the >=> operator.

### Code Examples

```js
// safeParseNum :: String -> Option Number
const safeParseNum = (b) => {
  const n = parseNumber(b)
  return isNaN(n) ? None() : Some(n)
}

// validatePositive :: Number -> Option Number
const validatePositive = (a) => a > 0 ? Some(a) : None()

// kleisliCompose :: Monad M => ((b -> M c), (a -> M b)) -> a -> M c
const kleisliCompose = (g, f) => (x) => f(x).chain(g)

// parseAndValidate :: String -> Option Number
const parseAndValidate = kleisliCompose(validatePositive, safeParseNum)

parseAndValidate('1') // => Some(1)
parseAndValidate('asdf') // => None
parseAndValidate('999') // => Some(999)
```

---

## Free Monad

- Category: Algebraic Structures
- ID: #free-monad
- Related concepts: #monad, #functor, #io, #algebraic-effects

### Definition
A Free Monad is a construction that builds a monad out of any functor without adding any domain-specific behavior. It cleanly separates the description of a program (an Abstract Syntax Tree of commands) from its execution (an interpreter that evaluates the AST).

### Code Examples

```js
// Free monad constructors:
const Pure = (x) => ({
  isPure: true,
  value: x,
  map: (f) => Pure(f(x)),
  chain: (f) => f(x)
})

const Free = (fn) => ({
  isPure: false,
  functor: fn,
  map: (f) => Free(fn.map((next) => next.map(f))),
  chain: (f) => Free(fn.map((next) => next.chain(f)))
})

// Lift an instruction functor into a Free monad:
const liftF = (cmd) => Free(cmd.map(Pure))

// Functor representing logging instructions:
const Log = (msg, next) => ({
  type: 'log',
  msg,
  next,
  map: (f) => Log(msg, f(next))
})

// Program: purely describes actions without executing them:
const logMsg = (msg) => liftF(Log(msg, null))
const program = logMsg('Starting').chain(() => logMsg('Done')).chain(() => Pure(42))

// Interpreter: executes the instruction tree:
const interpret = (freeMonad) => {
  if (freeMonad.isPure) return freeMonad.value
  const { type, msg, next } = freeMonad.functor
  if (type === 'log') {
    console.log(msg)
    return interpret(next)
  }
}

interpret(program) // Logs 'Starting', 'Done', returns 42
```

---

## Monad Transformer

- Category: Algebraic Structures
- ID: #monad-transformer
- Related concepts: #monad, #kleisli-composition, #either, #functor, #applicative-functor

### Definition
While functors and applicative functors compose naturally, monads do not compose generally without knowing their specific types. A Monad Transformer is a type constructor that takes an existing monad and produces a new monad with combined capabilities (such as combining error handling, asynchronous tasks, and state).

### Code Examples

```js
// MaybeT wraps any outer monad M to add optionality:
const MaybeT = (M) => {
  const of = (value) => MaybeTInstance(M.of({ isSome: true, value }))
  const none = () => MaybeTInstance(M.of({ isSome: false }))

  const MaybeTInstance = (run) => ({
    run,
    chain: (f) =>
      MaybeTInstance(
        run.chain((opt) => (opt.isSome ? f(opt.value).run : M.of(opt)))
      ),
    map: (f) =>
      MaybeTInstance(
        run.map((opt) => (opt.isSome ? { isSome: true, value: f(opt.value) } : opt))
      )
  })

  return { of, none, from: MaybeTInstance }
}

// Identity monad:
const Id = (x) => ({
  value: x,
  map: (f) => Id(f(x)),
  chain: (f) => f(x)
})
Id.of = Id

// Combine Id monad with Maybe effect:
const MaybeId = MaybeT(Id)

const findUser = (id) =>
  id === 1 ? MaybeId.of({ name: 'Alice', age: 30 }) : MaybeId.none()

const getAge = (id) =>
  findUser(id)
    .chain((user) => MaybeId.of(user.age))
    .run

getAge(1).value // { isSome: true, value: 30 }
getAge(2).value // { isSome: false }
```

---

## Applicative Functor

- Category: Algebraic Structures
- ID: #applicative-functor
- Aliases: applicative, ap
- Related concepts: #functor, #pointed-functor, #monad, #lift, #traversable, #alternative, #monad-transformer

### Definition
An applicative functor is an object with an ap function. ap applies a function in the object to a value in another object of the same type.

### Code Examples

```js
// Implementation
Array.prototype.ap = function (xs) {
  return this.reduce((acc, f) => acc.concat(xs.map(f)), [])
}

// Example usage
;[(a) => a + 1].ap([1]) // [2]
```

```js
// Arrays that you want to combine
const arg1 = [1, 3]
const arg2 = [4, 5]

// combining function - must be curried for this to work
const add = (x) => (y) => x + y

const partiallyAppliedAdds = [add].ap(arg1) // [(y) => 1 + y, (y) => 3 + y]
```

```js
partiallyAppliedAdds.ap(arg2) // [5, 6, 7, 8]
```

---

## Bifunctor

- Category: Algebraic Structures
- ID: #bifunctor
- Aliases: bimap, pair map
- Related concepts: #either, #functor, #product-type, #profunctor

### Definition
A structure with two independent type parameters that can map over both of them simultaneously. A Bifunctor provides bimap, which takes two functions and maps the first over the first type parameter and the second over the second type parameter.

### Code Examples

```js
const Pair = (first, second) => ({
  first,
  second,
  bimap: (f, g) => Pair(f(first), g(second)),
  firstMap: (f) => Pair(f(first), second),
  secondMap: (g) => Pair(first, g(second))
})

const score = Pair('alice', 10)
score.bimap((name) => name.toUpperCase(), (points) => points * 2)
// Pair('ALICE', 20)
```

---

## Contravariant Functor

- Category: Algebraic Structures
- ID: #contravariant-functor
- Aliases: contravariant, cmap, contramap
- Related concepts: #functor, #predicate, #profunctor

### Definition
A structure similar to a functor, but whose transformation flows in the opposite direction. While a covariant functor transforms a producer F<A> into F<B> via (a -> b), a contravariant functor transforms a consumer F<A> into F<B> via (b -> a) using cmap (or contramap).

### Code Examples

```js
// Predicate wraps a test function (x) -> Boolean
const Predicate = (test) => ({
  test,
  // cmap :: (b -> a) -> Predicate a -> Predicate b
  cmap: (f) => Predicate((x) => test(f(x)))
})

// An existing predicate checking if a string is long
const isLongString = Predicate((s) => s.length > 5)

// Contramap pre-processes a User object into a string (user.bio)
const hasLongBio = isLongString.cmap((user) => user.bio)

hasLongBio.test({ bio: 'Hello World' }) // true
hasLongBio.test({ bio: 'Hi' }) // false
```

---

## Profunctor

- Category: Algebraic Structures
- ID: #profunctor
- Related concepts: #bifunctor, #contravariant-functor, #lens

### Definition
A Profunctor is a bifunctor that is contravariant in its first argument and covariant in its second argument.

### Code Examples

```js
// Functions are natural profunctors:
const Profunctor = (fn) => ({
  run: fn,
  // promap :: (a' -> a) -> (b -> b') -> P a b -> P a' b'
  promap: (f, g) => Profunctor((x) => g(fn(f(x))))
})

// An existing function: String -> Number
const stringLength = Profunctor((str) => str.length)

// Pre-process input (trim whitespace) and post-process output (check if even):
const isTrimmedLengthEven = stringLength.promap(
  (raw) => raw.trim(), // contravariant: pre-process input
  (len) => len % 2 === 0 // covariant: post-process output
)

isTrimmedLengthEven.run('   code   ') // 4 is even -> true
isTrimmedLengthEven.run(' hello ') // 5 is odd -> false
```

---

## Alternative

- Category: Algebraic Structures
- ID: #alternative
- Aliases: alt, choice operator, fallback
- Related concepts: #applicative-functor, #monoid, #option

### Definition
An applicative functor that also forms a monoid, providing a binary choice operator alt (often written <|>) and an identity element for failure recovery and fallback logic.

### Code Examples

```js
const AltOption = {
  Some: (x) => ({
    alt: (_other) => AltOption.Some(x),
    value: x
  }),
  None: () => ({
    alt: (other) => other,
    value: null
  })
}

// Fallback configuration chain: first valid value wins
const primaryConfig = AltOption.None()
const secondaryConfig = AltOption.Some({ port: 8080 })
const defaultConfig = AltOption.Some({ port: 3000 })

const finalConfig = primaryConfig.alt(secondaryConfig).alt(defaultConfig)
finalConfig.value // { port: 8080 }
```

---

## Morphism

- Category: Category & Morphisms
- ID: #morphism
- Related concepts: #category, #homomorphism, #natural-transformation, #isomorphism

### Definition
A relationship between objects within a category. In the context of functional programming all functions are morphisms.

---

## Homomorphism

- Category: Category & Morphisms
- ID: #homomorphism
- Related concepts: #morphism, #endomorphism, #isomorphism, #monoid

### Definition
A function where there is a structural property that is the same in the input as well as the output.

### Code Examples

```js
// toList :: [number] -> string
const toList = (a) => a.join(', ')
```

---

## Endomorphism

- Category: Category & Morphisms
- ID: #endomorphism
- Related concepts: #homomorphism

### Definition
A function where the input type is the same as the output. Since the types are identical, endomorphisms are also homomorphisms.

### Code Examples

```js
// uppercase :: String -> String
const uppercase = (str) => str.toUpperCase()

// decrement :: Number -> Number
const decrement = (x) => x - 1
```

---

## Isomorphism

- Category: Category & Morphisms
- ID: #isomorphism
- Related concepts: #homomorphism, #iso, #morphism

### Definition
A morphism made of a pair of transformations between 2 types of objects that is structural in nature and no data is lost.

### Code Examples

```js
// Providing functions to convert in both directions makes the 2D coordinate structures isomorphic.
const pairToCoords = (pair) => ({ x: pair[0], y: pair[1] })

const coordsToPair = (coords) => [coords.x, coords.y]

coordsToPair(pairToCoords([1, 2])) // [1, 2]

pairToCoords(coordsToPair({ x: 1, y: 2 })) // {x: 1, y: 2}
```

---

## Catamorphism

- Category: Category & Morphisms
- ID: #catamorphism
- Aliases: fold, reduce, reduceright
- Related concepts: #anamorphism, #foldable, #hylomorphism, #paramorphism

### Definition
A function which deconstructs a structure into a single value. reduceRight is an example of a catamorphism for array structures.

### Code Examples

```js
// sum is a catamorphism from [Number] -> Number
const sum = xs => xs.reduceRight((acc, x) => acc + x, 0)

sum([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]) // 15
```

---

## Anamorphism

- Category: Category & Morphisms
- ID: #anamorphism
- Aliases: unfold, generate
- Related concepts: #catamorphism, #hylomorphism, #apomorphism

### Definition
A function that builds up a structure by repeatedly applying a function to its argument. unfold is an example which generates an array from a function and a seed value. This is the opposite of a catamorphism. You can think of this as an anamorphism builds up a structure and catamorphism breaks it down.

### Code Examples

```js
const unfold = (f, seed) => {
  function go (f, seed, acc) {
    const res = f(seed)
    return res ? go(f, res[1], acc.concat([res[0]])) : acc
  }
  return go(f, seed, [])
}
```

```js
const countDown = n => unfold((n) => {
  return n <= 0 ? undefined : [n, n - 1]
}, n)

countDown(5) // [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]
```

---

## Hylomorphism

- Category: Category & Morphisms
- ID: #hylomorphism
- Aliases: refold, unfold-then-fold
- Related concepts: #anamorphism, #catamorphism

### Definition
The function which composes an anamorphism followed by a catamorphism.

### Code Examples

```js
const sumUpToX = (x) => sum(countDown(x))
sumUpToX(5) // 15
```

---

## Paramorphism

- Category: Category & Morphisms
- ID: #paramorphism
- Aliases: para, reductive history
- Related concepts: #catamorphism

### Definition
A function just like reduceRight. However, there's a difference:

### Code Examples

```js
// Obviously not safe for lists containing `undefined`,
// but good enough to make the point.
const para = (reducer, accumulator, elements) => {
  if (elements.length === 0) { return accumulator }

  const head = elements[0]
  const tail = elements.slice(1)

  return reducer(head, tail, para(reducer, accumulator, tail))
}

const suffixes = list => para(
  (x, xs, suffxs) => [xs, ...suffxs],
  [],
  list
)

suffixes([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]) // [[2, 3, 4, 5], [3, 4, 5], [4, 5], [5], []]
```

---

## Apomorphism

- Category: Category & Morphisms
- ID: #apomorphism
- Aliases: apo, early return unfold
- Related concepts: #anamorphism

### Definition
The opposite of paramorphism, just as anamorphism is the opposite of catamorphism. With paramorphism, you retain access to the accumulator and what has been accumulated, apomorphism lets you unfold with the potential to return early.

---

## Natural Transformation

- Category: Category & Morphisms
- ID: #natural-transformation
- Aliases: nat, functor transformation
- Related concepts: #functor, #morphism, #category

### Definition
A structure-preserving mapping between two functors, transforming F<A> into G<A> without altering or inspecting the underlying value A.

### Code Examples

```js
// nat :: F a -> G a
// e.g. Array to Option (taking the head element)
const listToOption = (arr) => (arr.length > 0 ? { value: arr[0], isSome: true } : { value: null, isSome: false })

const double = (x) => x * 2

// Naturality law: transforming after map equals mapping after transform
const arrayTransformed = listToOption([1, 2, 3].map(double)) // { value: 2, isSome: true }
const mappedOption = { value: double(listToOption([1, 2, 3]).value), isSome: true } // { value: 2, isSome: true }
arrayTransformed.value === mappedOption.value // true
```

---

## Setoid

- Category: Algebraic Structures
- ID: #setoid
- Related concepts: #semigroup

### Definition
An object that has an equals function which can be used to compare other objects of the same type.

### Code Examples

```js
Array.prototype.equals = function (arr) {
  const len = this.length
  if (len !== arr.length) {
    return false
  }
  for (let i = 0; i < len; i++) {
    if (this[i] !== arr[i]) {
      return false
    }
  }
  return true
}

;[1, 2].equals([1, 2]) // true
;[1, 2].equals([0]) // false
```

---

## Semigroup

- Category: Algebraic Structures
- ID: #semigroup
- Related concepts: #monoid, #setoid, #semigroupoid

### Definition
An object that has a concat function that combines it with another object of the same type.

### Code Examples

```js
;[1].concat([2]) // [1, 2]
```

---

## Foldable

- Category: Algebraic Structures
- ID: #foldable
- Related concepts: #catamorphism, #monoid, #traversable

### Definition
An object that has a reduce function that applies a function against an accumulator and each element in the array (from left to right) to reduce it to a single value.

### Code Examples

```js
const sum = (list) => list.reduce((acc, val) => acc + val, 0)
sum([1, 2, 3]) // 6
```

---

## Traversable

- Category: Algebraic Structures
- ID: #traversable
- Aliases: sequence, traverse
- Related concepts: #foldable, #functor, #applicative-functor, #traversal

### Definition
A Foldable and Functor that can turn a collection of wrapped values inside-out via sequence or traverse, transforming F<G<A>> into G<F<A>>.

### Code Examples

```js
// sequence transforms a list of Promises into a Promise of a list
// [Promise<1>, Promise<2>] -> Promise<[1, 2]>
const promiseSequence = (promises) =>
  promises.reduce(
    (acc, p) => acc.then((arr) => p.then((val) => [...arr, val])),
    Promise.resolve([])
  )

promiseSequence([
  Promise.resolve(1),
  Promise.resolve(2),
  Promise.resolve(3)
]).then(console.log) // [1, 2, 3]
```

---

## Lens

- Category: Types & Data Modeling
- ID: #lens
- Aliases: getter, setter, optics
- Related concepts: #function-composition, #pure-function, #prism, #iso, #profunctor, #traversal

### Definition
A lens is a structure (often an object or function) that pairs a getter and a non-mutating setter for some other data structure.

### Code Examples

```js
// Using [Ramda's lens](http://ramdajs.com/docs/#lens)
const nameLens = R.lens(
  // getter for name property on an object
  (obj) => obj.name,
  // setter for name property
  (val, obj) => Object.assign({}, obj, { name: val })
)
```

```js
const person = { name: 'Gertrude Blanch' }

// invoke the getter
R.view(nameLens, person) // 'Gertrude Blanch'

// invoke the setter
R.set(nameLens, 'Shafi Goldwasser', person) // {name: 'Shafi Goldwasser'}

// run a function on the value in the structure
R.over(nameLens, uppercase, person) // {name: 'GERTRUDE BLANCH'}
```

```js
// This lens focuses on the first item in a non-empty array
const firstLens = R.lens(
  // get first item in array
  xs => xs[0],
  // non-mutating setter for first item in array
  (val, [__, ...xs]) => [val, ...xs]
)

const people = [{ name: 'Gertrude Blanch' }, { name: 'Shafi Goldwasser' }]

// Despite what you may assume, lenses compose left-to-right.
R.over(compose(firstLens, nameLens), uppercase, people) // [{'name': 'GERTRUDE BLANCH'}, {'name': 'Shafi Goldwasser'}]
```

---

## Prism

- Category: Types & Data Modeling
- ID: #prism
- Aliases: affine traversal, sum optics
- Related concepts: #lens, #sum-type, #option, #iso, #traversal

### Definition
An optic that focuses on a sub-case or variant of a sum type. Unlike a Lens, which always assumes the target field exists on a product structure, a Prism may fail to match because the target variant might not be present.

### Code Examples

```js
const Prism = (preview, review) => ({
  preview,
  review
})

// A prism focusing on numeric string values
const integerPrism = Prism(
  (str) => (/^-?\d+$/.test(str) ? Number(str) : null),
  (num) => String(num)
)

integerPrism.preview('42') // 42
integerPrism.preview('hello') // null
integerPrism.review(42) // '42'
```

---

## Iso

- Category: Types & Data Modeling
- ID: #iso
- Aliases: isomorphism optic, lossless conversion, reversible mapping
- Related concepts: #lens, #prism, #isomorphism

### Definition
An optic that defines a lossless, reversible two-way mapping between two representations of the same information (s and a). An Iso consists of a to function (s -> a) and a from function (a -> s) such that from(to(x)) === x and to(from(y)) === y.

### Code Examples

```js
const Iso = (to, from) => ({
  to,
  from
})

// Conversion between Celsius and Fahrenheit
const tempIso = Iso(
  (c) => (c * 9) / 5 + 32, // to Fahrenheit
  (f) => ((f - 32) * 5) / 9 // from Fahrenheit
)

tempIso.to(100) // 212
tempIso.from(212) // 100
```

---

## Traversal

- Category: Types & Data Modeling
- ID: #traversal
- Related concepts: #lens, #prism, #traversable

### Definition
An optic that focuses on zero, one, or multiple values (0..*) inside a data structure simultaneously.

### Code Examples

```js
const Traversal = (getAll, modify) => ({
  getAll,
  modify
})

// Traversal focusing only on even numbers in an array:
const evenTraversal = Traversal(
  (arr) => arr.filter((n) => n % 2 === 0),
  (f, arr) => arr.map((n) => (n % 2 === 0 ? f(n) : n))
)

const numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]

evenTraversal.getAll(numbers) // [2, 4, 6]
evenTraversal.modify((n) => n * 10, numbers) // [1, 20, 3, 40, 5, 60]
```

---

## Type Signatures

- Category: Types & Data Modeling
- ID: #type-signatures
- Related concepts: #contracts

### Definition
Often functions in JavaScript will include comments that indicate the types of their arguments and return values.

### Code Examples

```js
// functionName :: firstArgType -> secondArgType -> returnType

// add :: Number -> Number -> Number
const add = (x) => (y) => x + y

// increment :: Number -> Number
const increment = (x) => x + 1
```

```js
// call :: (a -> b) -> a -> b
const call = (f) => (x) => f(x)
```

```js
// map :: (a -> b) -> [a] -> [b]
const map = (f) => (list) => list.map(f)
```

---

## Algebraic data type

- Category: Types & Data Modeling
- ID: #algebraic-data-type
- Aliases: adt
- Related concepts: #sum-type, #product-type

### Definition
A composite type made from putting other types together. Two common classes of algebraic types are sum and product.

---

## Sum type

- Category: Types & Data Modeling
- ID: #sum-type
- Aliases: union type, discriminated union, tagged union
- Related concepts: #algebraic-data-type, #option, #either, #prism

### Definition
A Sum type is the combination of two types together into another one. It is called sum because the number of possible values in the result type is the sum of the input types.

### Code Examples

```js
// imagine that rather than sets here we have types that can only have these values
const bools = new Set([true, false])
const halfTrue = new Set(['half-true'])

// The weakLogic type contains the sum of the values from bools and halfTrue
const weakLogicValues = new Set([...bools, ...halfTrue])
```

---

## Product type

- Category: Types & Data Modeling
- ID: #product-type
- Aliases: tuple, pair, record, struct
- Related concepts: #algebraic-data-type, #bifunctor

### Definition
A product type combines types together in a way you're probably more familiar with:

### Code Examples

```js
// point :: (Number, Number) -> {x: Number, y: Number}
const point = (x, y) => ({ x, y })
```

---

## Option

- Category: Types & Data Modeling
- ID: #option
- Aliases: maybe, some, none, just, nothing
- Related concepts: #monad, #dealing-with-partial-functions, #sum-type, #either, #prism, #alternative, #functor, #kleisli-composition

### Definition
Option is a sum type with two cases often called Some and None.

### Code Examples

```js
// Naive definition

const Some = (v) => ({
  val: v,
  map (f) {
    return Some(f(this.val))
  },
  chain (f) {
    return f(this.val)
  }
})

const None = () => ({
  map (f) {
    return this
  },
  chain (f) {
    return this
  }
})

// maybeProp :: (String, {a}) -> Option a
const maybeProp = (key, obj) => typeof obj[key] === 'undefined' ? None() : Some(obj[key])
```

```js
// getItem :: Cart -> Option CartItem
const getItem = (cart) => maybeProp('item', cart)

// getPrice :: Item -> Option Number
const getPrice = (item) => maybeProp('price', item)

// getNestedPrice :: cart -> Option a
const getNestedPrice = (cart) => getItem(cart).chain(getPrice)

getNestedPrice({}) // None()
getNestedPrice({ item: { foo: 1 } }) // None()
getNestedPrice({ item: { price: 9.99 } }) // Some(9.99)
```

---

## Either

- Category: Types & Data Modeling
- ID: #either
- Aliases: result, left and right, right is right
- Related concepts: #option, #sum-type, #monad, #bifunctor, #monad-transformer, #pure-function

### Definition
A sum type with two cases, Left and Right. By convention, Right represents a successful computation and Left contains an error or failure reason ("right is right").

### Code Examples

```js
const Left = (x) => ({
  value: x,
  map: (_f) => Left(x),
  chain: (_f) => Left(x),
  fold: (f, _g) => f(x),
  isLeft: true
})

const Right = (x) => ({
  value: x,
  map: (f) => Right(f(x)),
  chain: (f) => f(x),
  fold: (_f, g) => g(x),
  isRight: true
})

// parseJson :: String -> Either String Object
const parseJson = (str) => {
  try {
    return Right(JSON.parse(str))
  } catch (err) {
    return Left(err.message)
  }
}

parseJson('{"user": "hemanth"}').map((obj) => obj.user) // Right('hemanth')
parseJson('invalid json').map((obj) => obj.user) // Left('Unexpected token...')
```

---

## Function

- Category: Core Functions
- ID: #function
- Related concepts: #pure-function, #lambda, #referential-transparency, #side-effects, #partial-function

### Definition
A function f :: A => B is an expression - often called arrow or lambda expression - with exactly one (immutable) parameter of type A and exactly one return value of type B. That value depends entirely on the argument, making functions context-independent, or referentially transparent. What is implied here is that a function must not produce any hidden side effects - a function is always pure, by definition. These properties make functions pleasant to work with: they are entirely deterministic and therefore predictable. Functions enable working with code as data, abstracting over behaviour:

### Code Examples

```js
// times2 :: Number -> Number
const times2 = n => n * 2

;[1, 2, 3].map(times2) // [2, 4, 6]
```

---

## Partial function

- Category: Core Functions
- ID: #partial-function
- Related concepts: #total-function, #dealing-with-partial-functions, #function

### Definition
A partial function is a function which is not defined for all arguments - it might return an unexpected result or may never terminate. Partial functions add cognitive overhead, they are harder to reason about and can lead to runtime errors. Some examples:

### Code Examples

```js
// example 1: sum of the list
// sum :: [Number] -> Number
const sum = arr => arr.reduce((a, b) => a + b)
sum([1, 2, 3]) // 6
sum([]) // TypeError: Reduce of empty array with no initial value

// example 2: get the first item in list
// first :: [A] -> A
const first = a => a[0]
first([42]) // 42
first([]) // undefined
// or even worse:
first([[42]])[0] // 42
first([])[0] // Uncaught TypeError: Cannot read property '0' of undefined

// example 3: repeat function N times
// times :: Number -> (Number -> Number) -> Number
const times = n => fn => n && (fn(n), times(n - 1)(fn))
times(3)(console.log)
// 3
// 2
// 1
times(-1)(console.log)
// RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
```

---

## Dealing with partial functions

- Category: Core Functions
- ID: #dealing-with-partial-functions
- Related concepts: #partial-function, #option

### Definition
Partial functions are dangerous as they need to be treated with great caution. You might get an unexpected (wrong) result or run into runtime errors. Sometimes a partial function might not return at all. Being aware of and treating all these edge cases accordingly can become very tedious. Fortunately a partial function can be converted to a regular (or total) one. We can provide default values or use guards to deal with inputs for which the (previously) partial function is undefined. Utilizing the Option type, we can yield either Some(value) or None where we would otherwise have behaved unexpectedly:

### Code Examples

```js
// example 1: sum of the list
// we can provide default value so it will always return result
// sum :: [Number] -> Number
const sum = arr => arr.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0)
sum([1, 2, 3]) // 6
sum([]) // 0

// example 2: get the first item in list
// change result to Option
// first :: [A] -> Option A
const first = a => a.length ? Some(a[0]) : None()
first([42]).map(a => console.log(a)) // 42
first([]).map(a => console.log(a)) // console.log won't execute at all
// our previous worst case
first([[42]]).map(a => console.log(a[0])) // 42
first([]).map(a => console.log(a[0])) // won't execute, so we won't have error here
// more of that, you will know by function return type (Option)
// that you should use `.map` method to access the data and you will never forget
// to check your input because such check become built-in into the function

// example 3: repeat function N times
// we should make function always terminate by changing conditions:
// times :: Number -> (Number -> Number) -> Number
const times = n => fn => n > 0 && (fn(n), times(n - 1)(fn))
times(3)(console.log)
// 3
// 2
// 1
times(-1)(console.log)
// won't execute anything
```

---

## Total Function

- Category: Core Functions
- ID: #total-function
- Related concepts: #partial-function

### Definition
A function which returns a valid result for all inputs defined in its type. This is as opposed to Partial Functions which may throw an error, return an unexpected result, or fail to terminate.

---

## Functional Programming Libraries in JavaScript

- Category: Types & Data Modeling
- ID: #functional-programming-libraries-in-javascript

### Definition
A curated catalog of functional programming libraries and toolkits in JavaScript including Ramda, Folktale, Sanctuary, and fp-ts.
